Field studies on the Softhead sea catfish (Notarius rugispinis) in estuarine habitats of northern South America have provided detailed life-history data for this commercially important ariid. Eggs are relatively large, with a recorded diameter of 14.5 mm, a feature that confers substantial yolk reserves for the developing embryo. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva emerges with an initial wet weight of 2.14 grams [Wwb = 2.14 grams], a substantial mass that reflects this large egg size and supports an extended endotrophic period during which the prolarva remains dependent on endogenous nutrients. The incubation temperature throughout embryonic development was maintained at 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], reflecting the stable thermal conditions of the coastal lagoon system where the species spawns. Following yolk absorption and the transition to exogenous feeding, the actively growing larva enters a pelagic larval phase that lasts several weeks before metamorphosis and subsequent settlement into demersal juvenile habitats.

As the juvenile fish progresses through its sub-adult phase, somatic growth follows a predictable allometric trajectory typical of demersal ariids. Puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the initiation of gametogenesis, is attained at a modest body length of 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters]. The corresponding body mass at this developmental milestone is approximately 122 grams [Wwp = approximately 122 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this population. This relatively early maturation, occurring at less than half the species' ultimate length, suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward ensuring reproductive output before potential mortality from predators or environmental variability. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Notarius grandicassis reveal that Softhead sea catfish reaches sexual maturity at a smaller size, potentially reflecting adaptation to more turbid, food-limited estuarine environments where rapid attainment of reproductive capacity is advantageous.

Reproductive output in the Softhead sea catfish is strongly influenced by the prevailing water temperature, which in this study was consistently recorded at 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C] throughout the spawning season. Under these thermal conditions, which favor optimal gonadal development and gamete quality, females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing 35 fertilised ova [N_R_i = each clutch containing 35 fertilised ova]. This iteroparous strategy, characterized by a single annual spawning event of moderate fecundity, is typical of ariids that provide parental care via oral incubation, a behavior that limits the number of offspring that can be successfully brooded at any one time. The reproductive cycle is synchronized with the onset of the rainy season, when increased freshwater inflow creates favorable salinity gradients for egg survival and larval dispersal into productive mangrove nursery areas. This temporal coupling ensures that hatchlings encounter abundant planktonic prey during the critical transition to exogenous feeding.

Males of the species exhibit pronounced oral incubation, carrying the embryos in their buccal cavity until eclosion. The maximum recorded total length attained by adult individuals in this population is 58.5 centimeters [Li = 58.5 centimeters], representing the ultimate size achieved after somatic growth has effectively ceased. The corresponding asymptotic body mass, calculated from the species-specific length-weight conversion, is 1672 grams [Wwi = 1672 grams], a value consistent with the upper range reported for estuarine ariids. This substantial terminal size, combined with the male's brooding commitment, imposes a significant energetic burden on larger individuals, which must balance the metabolic costs of maintaining body condition during the extended fasting period of mouthbrooding with the demands of territory defense and courtship. The trade-off between investment in current reproduction and future survival is particularly evident in this species, given the long incubation period required for the development of the yolk-rich eggs.

Longevity data, gathered from mark-recapture studies and otolith annuli readings conducted at the same experimental site maintained at 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], indicate that the maximum lifespan for Notarius rugispinis is 10 years [am = 10 years]. This moderate lifespan, intermediate between short-lived coastal opportunists and longer-lived deep-water ariids, aligns with a life-history syndrome characterized by delayed senescence and repeated reproductive events over the adult phase. The oldest documented individuals, approaching this maximum age, typically show reduced fecundity and slower growth rates, indicative of reproductive senescence. The combination of early puberty at 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters] total length and a maximum lifespan approaching a decade allows the species to buffer against sporadic recruitment failures by distributing reproductive effort across multiple years, a particularly advantageous strategy in the variable and periodically hypoxic estuarine environments this catfish inhabits.
